beats: A Russian judge died because he wanted perfect curtains!
His colleagues' first thought was who would get his job.
This is The Death of Ivan Ilych, by Leo Tolstoy.
The judge did everything right: good career, proper wife, fashionable furniture.
His life was simple, ordinary, and therefore terrible.
Then came a big promotion, and a grand new home to decorate.
Showing the upholsterer how to hang drapes, he climbed a ladder, slipped, and banged his side on a window knob.
Just a bruise. Then a strange taste. Then a pain that never left.
Doctors debated a floating kidney or the appendix. Nobody said dying.
His family pretended he was just sick, and that lie hurt worse than the pain.
Only the servant Gerasim told the truth, and held his master's legs on his shoulders all night.
For his last three days, he screamed.
Then his schoolboy son kissed his hand, and he pitied them all.
He looked for his fear of death, and found light instead!
Tolstoy's point: you can do everything right, and still live your whole life wrong.
Then he died, and his colleagues went back to playing cards.
